author: tom
title: Decimal odds: what the number actually means
dek: Decimal odds show your total return per dollar. Here is how to read them and what they say about probability.
body:
Australian bookmakers show decimal odds. The number is your total return, including your stake, for every dollar you bet. Once you know how to read it, the same number also tells you how likely the bookmaker thinks an outcome is, and how much margin is built into the price.

Reading the number

Multiply your stake by the odds to get your total return if the bet wins. Subtract the stake to get the profit.

Odds$10 bet returnsProfit
1.50$15$5
2.00$20$10
2.50$25$15
6.00$60$50

Odds of 2.00 are often called "even money": you double your stake. Anything below 2.00 is shorter than even money, meaning the outcome is considered more likely than not.

Odds and probability

Divide 1 by the odds to see the probability the price implies. Odds of 2.50 imply 40 per cent, because 1 ÷ 2.50 = 0.40. Odds of 1.25 imply 80 per cent; odds of 10.00 imply 10 per cent.

This is the bookmaker's view, not a fact. It is useful because it lets you compare a price with your own judgement. If you think a team has a 50 per cent chance and the odds are 2.50, the price implies only 40 per cent.

The bookmaker's margin

Add up the implied probabilities of every outcome in a market and you will get more than 100 per cent. The extra is the margin, sometimes called the overround, and it is how bookmakers make money over time.

In a two-team match priced at 1.90 and 1.90, each side implies 52.6 per cent, for a total of 105.2 per cent. The margin is about 5 per cent. Multis multiply margins together, which is why a multi with many legs carries a much larger margin than a single bet. Our guide to same-game multis explains how that works when the legs come from one match.

Other formats you may see

  • Fractional odds, used in the UK and Ireland, show profit relative to stake: 3/2 is the same as decimal 2.50.
  • American odds use plus and minus signs: +150 equals decimal 2.50, and −200 equals decimal 1.50.

Australian apps let you switch formats in settings, but decimal is the standard and the easiest to calculate with.

The takeaway

Read odds as total return per dollar, divide 1 by them to see the implied chance, and remember that every price includes a margin. Short odds do not make a bet safe, and long odds do not make it good value. Decide your stake before you look at the price.
